query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticle stability at high service temperatures is governed by the degree of lattice distortion in near‐equiatomic solid solutions, which promotes sluggish diffusion and suppresses phase separation and elemental segregation under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near‐equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles with moderate lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Intentionally increase the lattice distortion by designing an alloy with a larger spread in atomic radii or adding a minor proportion of a size-mismatched element.
generation.conditions: Exposure to catalytic conditions in the range of 773–1173 K and thermoelectric operating temperatures from 473–1923 K in an inert or mildly oxidizing environment.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice strain and the resulting disordered atomic energy landscape that slows atomic diffusion and impedes the growth of secondary phases.
generation.mechanism: Higher lattice distortion creates a rough energy landscape that reduces atom mobility (i.e., promotes sluggish diffusion), thereby maintaining high configurational entropy and inhibiting both phase separation and chemical segregation even under prolonged thermal stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles engineered with increased lattice distortion will show reduced coarsening, less elemental segregation, and a more stable single-phase structure compared to baseline particles; these effects should be observable via high-resolution imaging and elemental mapping after thermal aging tests.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles with moderate lattice distortion (using elements with similar atomic radii) that are prone to mild phase separation and elemental segregation under identical service conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to single-phase nanoparticles operating within 473–1923 K and may not hold if excessive lattice strain induces premature mechanical instability or if additional external factors (e.g., severe oxidation) dominate the degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: While lattice distortion is expected to slow diffusion, the precise quantitative relation between distortion magnitude and stability under catalytic versus thermoelectric conditions remains uncertain and may be complicated by surface effects in nanoparticles.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of near-equiatomic nanoparticles: one with a high degree of lattice distortion (by incorporating elements with significantly different atomic radii) and a control set with moderate lattice distortion. Subject both sets to prolonged thermal aging at 800–1000 K (for catalytic simulation) and 473–1200 K (for thermoelectric simulation) under controlled atmospheres. Structural stability will be evaluated before and after aging.
measurements: High-resolution TEM/SEM to track particle morphology and coarsening.
EDS mapping or atom probe tomography to assess elemental segregation.
XRD to verify phase stability and detect any secondary phase formation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with increased lattice distortion do not exhibit significantly lower degrees of coarsening, phase separation, or elemental segregation compared to the baseline nanoparticles under identical thermal aging conditions, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion governs structural and chemical stability under service regimes would be falsified.

System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25) BCC refractory high-entropy alloy. Question: Can refractory high-entropy alloy WTaMoNbV be adequately synthesized via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material, and how do its properties compare to a counterpart produced by arc melting furnace (AMF)?. System: Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV (20 at.% W, 20 at.% Ta, 20 at.% Mo, 20 at.% Nb, 20 at.% V). Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using EOSINT M290 system (400 W Nd-YAG laser, pure argon atmosphere); mixed elemental powders (20–70 µm) stirred for 6 h at 23 rpm; advanced trials parameters: 244 W laser power, 300 mm/s scanning speed, 0.10 mm hatch spacing, 0.03 mm layer thickness, 162.7 J/mm³ energy density, 67° layer rotation.. Test conditions: Density and Vickers hardness (HV10) measured; compression strength tested at 0.5 mm/min crosshead speed; electrochemical behavior assessed via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl solution at ambient temperature (scanning rate 0.5 mV/s)..
